name: March 1989 Quebec Blackout

phenomena.details: AR 5395 produced an X15 flare on March 6, 1989 (one of the largest of the cycle); the geoeffective driver of the March 13 storm was the region's later activity, including an X4.5 flare on March 10.
Fast CME ~1500 km/s; transit time ~3.5 days.
Dst −589 nT, Kp 9 (9−); one of the largest storms of the 20th century.
Major solar energetic particle event; proton flux >10 MeV exceeded 40,000 pfu.

impacts.description: The Hydro-Québec power grid collapsed within 92 seconds as GICs tripped relay protection systems in a cascading failure; 6 million people lost power for up to 9 hours. Estimated economic loss ~$2 billion CAD.
Salem Nuclear Power Plant in New Jersey experienced transformer damage; at least 200 power system problems reported in the US including seven power transformer failures.
GOES-7 weather satellite lost about half its solar array capacity. Multiple satellite attitude control anomalies from electrostatic charging. NASA TDRS-1 experienced 250 anomalies in one day.
Aurora visible as far south as Florida, Cuba, and Mexico (~25° N latitude); seen across most of North America, Europe, and Asia.

papers.title: Geomagnetic disturbance and its effects on power systems
papers.journal: Journal of Atmospheric and Solar-Terrestrial Physics
papers.keyFinding: Detailed analysis of the Hydro-Québec cascade failure, finding the grid collapsed in 92 seconds due to GIC-induced relay misoperation, and recommending protective measures.

papers.title: The effects of geomagnetic disturbances on electrical systems at the earth's surface
papers.authors: Allen, J., Frank, L., Sauer, H., Reiff, P.
papers.keyFinding: Catalogued the extensive range of electrical and technological impacts of the March 1989 storm in the immediate aftermath.

papers.title: Reanalysis of the March 1989 great geomagnetic storm
papers.keyFinding: Revised storm chronology and GIC estimates, confirming the Quebec blackout mechanism and providing updated infrastructure vulnerability assessments.

summary: The March 13, 1989 geomagnetic storm (Dst −589 nT) drove geomagnetically induced currents that collapsed the Hydro-Québec power grid in 92 seconds, leaving 6 million people without electricity for up to 9 hours – the most significant space weather power grid failure in North American history.
description: Active region AR 5395 produced an X15 flare on March 6, 1989 – one of the largest of the cycle – and remained intensely active for days. A fast CME (approximately 1500 km/s) from the region's continued eruptions, including an X4.5 flare on March 10, arrived at Earth on March 13 and drove one of the most intense geomagnetic storms of the 20th century (Dst −589 nT, Kp 9). The resulting GICs overwhelmed relay protection systems in the Hydro-Québec power grid; in just 92 seconds, the entire 735-kV transmission system tripped, leaving approximately 6 million Québec residents without electricity. Power was restored to most within 9 hours, but some regions waited days. The storm simultaneously damaged transformers at the Salem Nuclear Power Plant in New Jersey and caused at least 200 other power system problems across North America. NASA's TDRS-1 communications satellite logged 250 anomalies in a single day, and GOES-7 lost half its solar array capacity. Aurora was visible as far south as Florida and Cuba at ~25° N geographic latitude. The event became the defining case study in power grid vulnerability to space weather and directly motivated new GIC protection standards.
